clue.text: Speaking likeness of Galatea

parts.note: Galatea was the carved figure Pygmalion made, which Venus brought to life; a 'speaking likeness' is a lifelike portrait, and she literally came to speak

explanation.surface: A portrait so true to Galatea that it seems to talk.
explanation.walkthrough: In the myth Pygmalion sculpted an ivory woman, later called Galatea, who came to life; 'speaking likeness' is both the idiom for a lifelike image and a carved figure that really did speak.
explanation.definitionFit: Galatea began as a carved figure of a woman, an image in ivory that came alive.

clue.text: "There are no faces than those that are so wash'd " (Much Ado About Nothing)

definitions.text: "There are no faces than those that are so wash'd " (Much Ado About Nothing)

parts.words: "There are no faces than those that are so wash'd " (Much Ado About Nothing)
parts.note: a quotation with its missing word dropped: the gap after 'no faces' wants a comparative adjective meaning more honest or genuine, from the first scene of Much Ado

explanation.walkthrough: In Much Ado About Nothing (Act 1, scene 1) Leonato says no faces are more honest than those washed with tears of joy; the missing comparative fills the line.
explanation.definitionFit: The quoted line compares faces for sincerity, so the gap takes the comparative of 'genuine' or 'honest'.

clue.text: Master Shallow also heard them at midnight

definitions.text: Master Shallow also heard them at midnight

parts.words: Master Shallow also heard them at midnight
parts.note: recalls Falstaff's line to Justice Shallow in Henry IV Part 2, 'We have heard ... at midnight, Master Shallow', and 'also' points to a Dickens Christmas book of the same name

explanation.surface: Old Justice Shallow, like Falstaff, remembers the bells ringing at twelve.
explanation.walkthrough: Falstaff tells Shallow 'We have heard the chimes at midnight' (Henry IV Part 2); 'also' hints that the phrase's last two words are a title too, Dickens's second Christmas book.
explanation.definitionFit: The bells striking twelve are what Falstaff and Shallow heard, and the same words title a Dickens Christmas story.

clue.text: Darkness to be traversed, before getting public transport?

parts.note: ere is a poetic word for before
a bus is a form of public transport

explanation.surface: A dark journey lies ahead, so take the bus before setting out.
explanation.walkthrough: Erebus is the primeval darkness of Greek myth, the gloomy region souls pass through on the way to Hades, hence 'to be traversed'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Erebus is the personified darkness of the underworld.

clue.text: Part of joint including New York's poet

indicators.note: the word for part of a joint takes in the abbreviation for New York's, holding it within

parts.note: a tenon is the projecting tongue of a mortise-and-tenon joint
NY is the abbreviation for New York, plus S for the possessive

explanation.surface: A New York poet is somehow part of a carpentry joint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'including' puts NYS inside TENON, split as TEN...ON.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred, Lord Tennyson was the Victorian Poet Laureate.

clue.text: Coxed pair? (to say nothing of the dog)

definitions.text: Coxed pair? (to say nothing of the dog)

parts.words: Coxed pair? (to say nothing of the dog)
parts.note: a rowing pair plus a cox makes a trio afloat, and the bracket quotes the subtitle of Jerome K. Jerome's comic novel about a Thames trip

explanation.surface: A rowing crew of two plus a cox, not counting the dog.
explanation.walkthrough: Jerome K. Jerome's 1889 novel is subtitled 'To Say Nothing of the Dog'; a coxed pair is two rowers and a cox, a trio on the water.
explanation.definitionFit: A coxed pair carries two rowers and a coxswain, a trio afloat, and the subtitle names Jerome's book.

clue.text: Role like Moll Flanders or Fanny Hill

definitions.text: Role like Moll Flanders or Fanny Hill

parts.words: Role like Moll Flanders or Fanny Hill
parts.note: both heroines give their names to the novels they appear in, so playing either is playing the title role

explanation.surface: Casting for one of two notorious eighteenth-century heroines.
explanation.walkthrough: Defoe's Moll Flanders and Cleland's Fanny Hill are both books named after their heroines; a part that gives a work its title has this name in theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: A title role, one that shares its name with the work, is called this in the theatre.

clue.text: Novelist, something of a lawyer by profession ()

indicators.note: only a part of the words lawyer by profession is wanted, a run of letters inside them

explanation.surface: A writer who was a lawyer by profession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'something of' signals a run hidden in lawYER BY profession.
explanation.definitionFit: Frank Yerby was an American writer of popular historical fiction.

clue.text: His life was enough to shame the devil

definitions.text: His life was enough to shame the devil

parts.words: His life was enough to shame the devil
parts.note: the Irish writer Liam who wrote the autobiography Shame the Devil (1934), so his life story bears that title

explanation.surface: A man so wicked his deeds would embarrass Satan.
explanation.walkthrough: Liam O'Flaherty called his 1934 autobiography Shame the Devil; the clue reads like a moral judgement but names the book of his life.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish novelist Liam wrote a memoir titled Shame the Devil, so his life story is that book.

clue.text: Somehow agree a menu for Bulwer Lytton's schoolmaster

indicators.note: the letters are to be put together in some other way, a rearranging signal

explanation.surface: A restaurant order for the schoolmaster in a Victorian novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somehow' rearranges AGREE A MENU. Bulwer Lytton's 1832 novel tells of the real schoolmaster-murderer of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Bulwer Lytton's novel is named after its usher-scholar hero, a teacher hanged for murder.

clue.text: Eric Linklater's was of honour

parts.note: the Scottish novelist wrote a book titled with a list of the honoured war dead, so the gap before 'of honour' wants that list's name

explanation.walkthrough: Eric Linklater's 1961 novel is 'Roll of Honour'; the clue drops the first word of the title.
explanation.definitionFit: A list or register of names, as in a list of honoured dead, gives Linklater's title.

clue.text: Beethoven trio badly received in Sarajevo?

definitions.meaning: Beethoven's Piano Trio in B flat, Op. 97, is nicknamed after its dedicatee Rudolph of Austria
Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austrian throne, was shot in Sarajevo in 1914

explanation.walkthrough: Both senses name a Habsburg title: Beethoven's patron Rudolph, and Franz Ferdinand, whose assassination in Sarajevo began the First World War.
explanation.definitionFit: Beethoven's Op. 97 trio is nicknamed after a Habsburg prince, and an Austrian prince of that rank was assassinated at Sarajevo.

clue.text: Deceptive bid from Beaumont and Shadwell

definitions.meaning: in bridge, a bluffing call made to mislead the opponents about one's hand
Joseph Beaumont wrote a long poem and Thomas Shadwell an opera, each titled after the mythical beloved of Cupid

explanation.walkthrough: A bridge player's bluff bid shares its name with the soul-maiden loved by Cupid, the subject of Beaumont's poem (1648) and Shadwell's opera (1675).
explanation.definitionFit: A bluff call at bridge has this name, and the beloved of Cupid titles works by both writers.

clue.text: The Annales Cambriae are partly a swindle

indicators.note: only part of the words Annales Cambriae is used, a run of letters crossing the two words

explanation.surface: A medieval Welsh chronicle accused of being a fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'partly' points to the run hidden in annaleS CAMbriae; the Annales Cambriae are early Welsh annals.
explanation.definitionFit: A con or fraud is a trick to cheat someone, a synonym of swindle.

clue.text: That of Richards was practical

parts.note: I. A. Richards's 1929 book on close reading was titled with the word practical followed by the gap's word

explanation.surface: Richards took a down-to-earth approach to something.
explanation.walkthrough: I. A. Richards's 'Practical Criticism' (1929) founded close reading in English studies.
explanation.definitionFit: Richards's book title names the judging of literary works, the practice of literary evaluation.

clue.text: Go wrong with worker on railway in search for adventure

parts.note: to err is to go wrong
the ant is the crossword's usual worker

explanation.surface: A railway worker makes a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: A worker is an ANT in crosswords; 'on' places it before RY in the across entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Knight-errantry is the roaming of a knight in quest of adventures.

clue.text: Stout fellow (emperor, novelist)

parts.note: Nero was a Roman emperor
Thomas Wolfe was an American novelist (Look Homeward, Angel)

explanation.surface: A sturdy chap who is both emperor and novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stout fellow' sounds like praise for a good chap, but it is Rex Stout's corpulent detective.
explanation.definitionFit: Rex Stout created this fat orchid-loving detective, so he is literally Stout's man.

clue.text: It's better to be — than honest " (Tom Stoppard)

definitions.text: It's better to be — than honest " (Tom Stoppard)

parts.words: It's better to be — than honest " (Tom Stoppard)
parts.note: a remark by the playwright, the dash standing for an adjective meaning worth repeating, set against being truthful

explanation.walkthrough: Stoppard's remark is 'It's better to be quotable than to be honest'; the dash marks the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: The line prefers being memorable and much repeated over truthful, an adjective for words worth citing.

clue.text: Twins in radio's curious item

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the words that follow, running across them

explanation.surface: A curious radio item about twins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points to the run hidden in raDIO'S CURIous; the Dioscuri are Castor and Pollux.
explanation.definitionFit: Castor and Pollux, the sons of Zeus, are the heavenly twin brothers known by this Greek name.

clue.text: Jean starts Rochester's history, yet stops

indicators.note: the beginnings of the four following words are taken, one letter from each

explanation.surface: Jean begins Rochester's story but then breaks off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts' takes the opening letters of Rochester's, history, yet, stops. Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea tells the backstory of Rochester's first wife from Jane Eyre.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean Rhys is the novelist who wrote Wide Sargasso Sea, so her first name points to her surname.

clue.text: Alter ego presented by Milton in

definitions.text: Alter ego presented by Milton in

parts.words: Alter ego presented by Milton in
parts.note: Milton, blind and among enemies after the Restoration, is widely read as portraying himself in the blinded Hebrew strongman of his closet drama Agonistes

explanation.walkthrough: The clue appears cut short after 'in' (presumably 'Agonistes'); Milton's blind captive hero in Samson Agonistes is often read as his own self-portrait.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton's blinded hero among the Philistines mirrors the blind poet himself, a second self.

clue.text: "I am as melancholy as a —, or a lugg'd bear" (Henry IV, Part I)

definitions.text: "I am as melancholy as a —, or a lugg'd bear" (Henry IV, Part I)

parts.words: "I am as melancholy as a —, or a lugg'd bear" (Henry IV, Part I)
parts.note: Falstaff's line in the second scene of the play, the gap wanting an old word for a tom, a castrated male feline

explanation.walkthrough: Falstaff says 'I am as melancholy as a gib-cat or a lugged bear' (Henry IV Part 1, Act 1 scene 2).
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for a tomcat, especially a gelded one, thought proverbially mopey.

clue.text: Song included by Joyce Oates ()

parts.note: the American novelist's full name has a middle name between Joyce and Oates, and that middle name is also a festive song

explanation.walkthrough: The novelist is Joyce Carol Oates, so the word between her names is 'included by' them and also means a Christmas song.
explanation.definitionFit: A carol is a joyful hymn, especially at Christmas, and is the middle name of the writer.

clue.text: First man on fish-trap in Stevenson book

parts.note: Adam was the first man in Genesis
a weir is a fence or enclosure set in a river to catch fish

explanation.surface: Adam standing on a fish-trap in a Stevenson tale.
explanation.walkthrough: Adam Weir is the hanging judge, Lord Hermiston, in Stevenson's unfinished Weir of Hermiston.
explanation.definitionFit: The stern Lord Justice-Clerk father in Stevenson's last novel, Weir of Hermiston, bears this name.

clue.text: Oscar's sort of mate ()

parts.note: Oscar Wilde wrote a comedy about a perfect spouse, whose title describes the kind of husband in it

explanation.surface: The kind of friend Oscar would choose.
explanation.walkthrough: Oscar Wilde's play is 'An Ideal Husband'; 'mate' here means a spouse.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilde's husband is perfect in title, so his sort of spouse is the perfect one.

clue.text: Billy, undertaker's clerk addicted to pork pies

definitions.text: Billy, undertaker's clerk addicted to pork pies

parts.words: Billy, undertaker's clerk addicted to pork pies
parts.note: Keith Waterhouse's hero Billy Fisher works for undertakers and tells endless tall tales; 'pork pies' is rhyming slang for lies

explanation.surface: An undertaker's clerk named Billy who cannot stop eating pork pies.
explanation.walkthrough: Billy Liar (Keith Waterhouse, 1959) is a fantasist clerk at an undertaker's; 'pork pies' is Cockney rhyming slang for lies, so he is addicted to telling them.
explanation.definitionFit: Billy Fisher's surname-nickname means a teller of untruths, which he is by habit.

clue.text: A generous, liberal-minded man, according to Dr Johnson

definitions.text: A generous, liberal-minded man, according to Dr Johnson

parts.words: A generous, liberal-minded man, according to Dr Johnson
parts.note: Johnson, often dependent on the trade, defended book traders as generous, liberal-minded men

explanation.walkthrough: Johnson, in Boswell's Life, called the publishers and sellers of books 'generous, liberal-minded men'; the clue reads like a general compliment.
explanation.definitionFit: Johnson's praise was for the trade that sells and publishes volumes, the dealer in printed works.

clue.text: Tobias Smelfungus, Doctor of Men and Manners

definitions.text: Tobias Smelfungus, Doctor of Men and Manners

parts.words: Tobias Smelfungus, Doctor of Men and Manners
parts.note: Sterne mocked a fellow novelist, the surgeon Tobias, as Smelfungus in A Sentimental Journey for his sour travel book

explanation.walkthrough: Sterne nicknamed the Scottish novelist and ship's surgeon Tobias Smollett 'Smelfungus' for his grumbling Travels through France and Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish novelist Tobias, trained as a surgeon and a satirist of manners, was Sterne's Smelfungus.

clue.text: Goading for Hodge in early play

definitions.meaning: in Gammer Gurton's ..., an early English comedy, Hodge's breeches cannot be mended until the lost sewing tool is found

explanation.walkthrough: Gammer Gurton's Needle (c. 1553) is one of the earliest English comedies; Hodge is the servant whose torn breeches wait on the lost needle.
explanation.definitionFit: To needle is to provoke or goad, and the early comedy turns on a lost sewing pin for Hodge's breeches.
